summary: Describes the goals and requirements for network mobility, which arises when a router moves with an entire network and its point of attachment to the Internet changes. The aim is to keep sessions between nodes in the mobile network and the wider Internet working during the move. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A train with Wi-Fi moves from one tower to another, yet everyone onboard wants to keep watching their video. This note lists what the solution must achieve.

questions: what are the goals of network mobility
how does nemo basic support work
subtitle: Keeping sessions alive when a mobile network changes where it connects to the Internet

tldr.problem: When a router connecting a network to the Internet moves (such as a train changing base station), all devices behind it lose their Internet sessions because the network's address prefix changes.
tldr.mechanism: NEMO Basic Support requires each mobile router to maintain a bi-directional tunnel with a Home Agent, preserving the network's address identity and allowing all traffic to flow through the tunnel regardless of where the router attaches.
tldr.outcome: All nodes in the mobile network stay reachable at their permanent addresses and maintain ongoing sessions, making the network's movement transparent to applications.

today: RFC 4886 is informational and defines the goals and requirements for NEMO. The Basic Support protocol (RFC 3963) has been implemented and deployed, particularly in scenarios involving vehicles, public transportation, and mobile hotspots. Extended Support work continues in the IETF for route optimization and more complex multihoming scenarios.

sections.title: Network Mobility and the NEMO Problem
sections.content:
Network mobility is different from host mobility. When a single mobile device (like a laptop) moves, only that device's connection needs to be maintained. When an entire network moves—such as a train's onboard Wi-Fi network, a vehicle with multiple computers, or a personal area network around a cell phone—the challenge is to keep all nodes in that network reachable and all sessions active.

A mobile network has one or more mobile routers that connect it to the Internet. Inside are mobile network nodes (MNNs), which can be fixed devices (like computers on a train) or mobile nodes (like passengers with laptops). When the mobile router moves and changes its attachment point to the Internet, the network's address prefix changes, which breaks all ongoing sessions unless the change is hidden.

The NEMO working group was formed to handle this problem. The solution uses concepts from Mobile IPv6 but extends them so that a single mobile router can represent an entire network.
sections.plainLanguage: A train has computers and Wi-Fi onboard. The train moves between cell towers, but everyone onboard should stay connected to the internet. NEMO keeps everyone's connections working even though the train keeps moving.

sections.title: Design Goals and Requirements
sections.content:
NEMO Basic Support has twelve main design goals that guide the solution. Migration transparency means all nodes stay reachable via permanent addresses. Performance transparency means handovers cause minimal packet loss or delay. Network mobility support transparency means only the mobile router needs to implement mobility, not the internal nodes.

Operational transparency requires the solution to work at the IP layer, invisible to upper-layer protocols. Arbitrary configurations means the solution must work for networks of any size, from simple (one router with one host) to complex (nested mobile networks, multihoming, thousands of devices).

The solution must also support secure signaling to prevent attackers from taking over the mobile network, handle location privacy so that correspondent nodes cannot determine the mobile network's topological location, and minimize impact on the global Internet routing system.

The solution must be backward compatible with IPv6 standards and allow host mobility (Mobile IPv6) to work correctly both inside and outside the mobile network.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone inside the network needs a permanent address. Moving should not lose connections. Only the router needs to know about mobility, not the devices inside. The solution works at the IP layer, invisible to apps. It must be secure and work with any network shape.

sections.title: Basic Support Solution Overview
sections.content:
NEMO Basic Support uses a straightforward approach: each mobile router has a Home Agent, just like a mobile device would in Mobile IPv6. When the mobile router moves and attaches to a new network, it acquires a Care-of Address at that new attachment point.

All traffic between nodes in the mobile network and correspondent nodes in the global Internet flows through a bi-directional tunnel between the mobile router and its Home Agent. This tunnel preserves the original network address prefix, making the network's movement invisible to the rest of the Internet.

The mobile router registers its Care-of Address with the Home Agent (using Mobile IPv6 mechanisms), and the Home Agent tunnels all traffic destined for the mobile network's prefix to the mobile router at its current location. Traffic from the mobile network is tunneled back to the Home Agent, which forwards it to the Internet.

This approach is simple and works for nested mobile networks: each mobile router can appear to its attachment point as a single node, allowing one mobile network to attach to another mobile network.
sections.plainLanguage: The router has a home office that always knows where it is. All traffic between the network and the internet goes through a tunnel to that home office. When the router moves, the home office updates where packets should go, but the network's address never changes from the internet's viewpoint.

sections.title: Detailed NEMO Basic Support Requirements
sections.content:
The NEMO Basic Support specification requires seventeen technical requirements. The solution must work at IP layer (R01) and establish a bi-directional tunnel between each mobile router and its Home Agent (R02). All traffic between mobile network nodes and correspondent nodes must flow through this tunnel (R03).

Mobile network nodes must remain reachable at permanent IP addresses (R04) and maintain continuous sessions across handovers (R05). The solution must not require changes to nodes other than mobile routers and Home Agents (R06), and must support fixed nodes, mobile hosts, and mobile routers inside the mobile network (R07).

The solution must support Mobile IPv6-enabled nodes using the mobile network as either a home link or foreign link (R08), ensure backward compatibility with all IETF standards including Mobile IPv6 (R09), and be agnostic to internal configuration—behaving the same whether the network is nested, contains multiple subnets, or has mixed node types (R10).

It must support at least two levels of nesting and arbitrary levels in principle (R11), work for multihomed mobile routers and networks (R12), minimize signaling (R13), secure all control messages (R14), ensure routing and management operations work over the tunnel (R15), preserve sessions when one interface fails (R16), and minimize impact on Internet routing (R17).
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of detailed requirements ensure the solution is secure, works with different network layouts, supports mobility features, and doesn't break other internet protocols. The main one is: keep everything working through the tunnel, regardless of how the network is structured.

sections.title: Future Work and Extended Support
sections.content:
NEMO Basic Support solves the core problem: maintaining sessions when a mobile network moves. However, NEMO Extended Support is being investigated for more optimal routing. When a mobile network moves, traffic may take suboptimal paths through the tunnel, especially with nested mobile networks.

Extended Support work explores optimizations such as route optimization (where correspondent nodes send packets directly to the mobile network rather than through the Home Agent tunnel) and improved multihoming scenarios. This work is ongoing in the IETF and is being investigated before standardization is pursued.

Security remains important: mobile networks introduce new challenges around authentication and preventing attacks. Existing IETF security solutions are reused where appropriate, and new security mechanisms are carefully designed to avoid introducing vulnerabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic solution works and is standardized. Future work will explore ways to make routing more efficient and handle more complex network shapes. Security is always being reviewed to prevent new attacks as mobile networks become more common.
